purpose: Dictionary of canonical marker names, synonyms, and measurement units. Required when building trends and comparing lab results. Different laboratories may report the same marker in different units; comparing raw values without checking units produces misleading trends.
rules: Always verify measurement units before comparing two values for the same marker.
If units differ, convert using the specified factor and clearly label the converted point, or compare positions within the reference intervals instead of absolute values.
Do not directly compare values from different laboratories: reference intervals depend on the method. Compare each value relative to its reference interval.
Markers listed in not_synonyms are different analytes and must never be merged into one trend.
Conversion factors marked assay_dependent are approximate and depend on the test system. If results conflict, use the laboratory reference interval rather than the conversion.
If a marker is absent from this dictionary, do not merge differently named markers into a trend without explicitly confirming that they are the same analyte.

markers.note: Highest-risk unit mismatch in the dataset: 6.5 ng/mL is approximately 22.5 nmol/L. Without conversion, 17.33 nmol/L to 6.5 ng/mL appears to be a threefold fall, but is actually an increase. Free testosterone is a separate analyte and must not be included in the total testosterone trend.
Blood and salivary cortisol are different analytes with different reference intervals and must not be merged. For salivary cortisol, the daily rhythm matters more than a single point.
12.6 pmol/L is approximately 0.98 ng/dL. Comparing a value in pmol/L against a reference interval in ng/dL creates an apparent sevenfold elevation and a false impression of thyrotoxicosis.
The factor depends on the assay and calibration standard. Use it as a guide; base the final assessment on the laboratory reference interval.
mIU/L and µIU/mL are numerically equivalent. No numerical conversion is needed, but normalize unit names so the points appear in the same trend.
µg/L and ng/mL are numerically equivalent.

synonyms: Total vitamin D (25-OH D2 and D3)
markers.note: The dataset currently uses one unit, but international sources often use nmol/L, so a conversion factor is needed when comparing with guidelines. Values above the reference interval suggest excessive intake, not deficiency.
The synonyms differ only in spelling.
Some records lack a unit. Treat a unitless value as mmol/L only if it is within 2–30; otherwise request clarification.
Whole-blood iron reported in µg/L is a separate analyte and must not be included in the serum iron trend.
10^9/L and x10^9/L are equivalent spellings. cells/µL requires conversion: 6500 cells/µL = 6.5 ×10⁹/L.
10^12/L and x10^12/L are equivalent spellings.
The unit spellings differ, but the units are equivalent.

CRITICAL: percentages and absolute counts are different measurements. The percentage can rise while the absolute count falls, and vice versa. Mixing them in one trend creates a false impression of lymphocytosis. The absolute count is clinically significant.
See the note for absolute lymphocytes.
Do not mix percentages with absolute counts.

Segmented neutrophils are a subset of total neutrophils; these are different measurements. An absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 ×10⁹/L is a critical value (agranulocytosis); see critical-values.md.
